One Perm resident, who was not identified, told Russian state television that the plane crashed directly in front of her home and produced an enormous blaze. She said it resembled fireworks. The force of the impact, she said, threw her across her bed sheets, after which her daughter rushed in from another room and asked whether a war had begun. She and other witnesses reported seeing the aircraft on fire before it fell. “It looked like a comet,” she said.

The flight had been traveling from Moscow to Perm when, shortly before landing at about 3:10 a.m. local time, or 2110 GMT, the pilots lost contact with air traffic controllers, an Aeroflot official said. He described conditions at the time as “mediocre.”

Yuri Orlov, the public safety minister for the Perm region, said investigators were searching across an area of roughly 2.5 miles, or 4 kilometers, covering homes and railway lines. He said it appeared the aircraft was already burning at an altitude of one kilometer, after which communications stopped and the plane exploded.

Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin said the flight data recorder had been found and would be examined by the International Aviation Commission.

The aircraft was carrying 82 passengers — seven of them children — along with six crew members. Koshlyakov said at least 21 foreign nationals were on the plane, including people traveling on passports from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland, and Ukraine. The U.S. Embassy said no Americans were aboard, despite one passenger having been listed as a U.S. citizen.

The crash was the second involving a Boeing 737 in the region in under a month. On August 24, a Boeing 737 bound for Iran crashed just outside the airport in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, with 90 people on board; 68 were killed.

The Boeing 737 is one of the most widely used aircraft in commercial aviation, with thousands operating worldwide. Aeroflot said the plane that crashed in Perm had been built in 1992 and was flown by its subsidiary, Aeroflot-Nord. Koshlyakov said the aircraft had all required certifications and added that Aeroflot carries out audits and inspections of affiliated companies to evaluate aircraft effectiveness, safety, and reliability.

The aircraft, operating as **Aeroflot-Nord Flight 821**, was flying from Moscow to Perm when it went down shortly before landing, breaking apart and bursting into flames near a section of the Trans-Siberian Railway. Authorities said the dead included **82 passengers and six crew members**. There were no survivors.

Emergency officials said the crash scattered wreckage over a wide area and temporarily disrupted rail traffic after debris fell near the tracks. Rescue teams, firefighters and investigators worked through the morning at the crash site, where sections of the fuselage were charred and fragmented.

“I heard the plane flying very low, then there was a flash and a bang,” one witness told local media. Others described seeing the aircraft descend at an unusual angle before it struck the ground and erupted in flames.

Initial reports indicated the crew had been preparing to land when contact with air traffic controllers was lost. The aircraft reportedly failed to complete its final approach and crashed after deviating from its expected flight path.

Later findings by Russian investigators concluded that the crash was caused primarily by **loss of control after the pilots became spatially disoriented**, meaning they misinterpreted the aircraft’s attitude and motion. The investigation also cited **insufficient crew training, poor cockpit coordination and difficulties handling the Boeing’s Western-style instruments** as contributing factors.

Investigators also reported that the captain had **alcohol in his system**, though the broader cause of the crash was attributed to a combination of human factors, training deficiencies and operational oversight.

### Black boxes recovered

Search crews recovered the aircraft’s **flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder**, commonly known as black boxes, and sent them for analysis. Investigators from Russia’s Interstate Aviation Committee led the inquiry, with assistance from aviation experts and representatives connected to the aircraft’s manufacturer.

The Boeing 737-500 involved in the crash was operated by **Aeroflot-Nord**, a regional subsidiary affiliated with Russia’s flagship carrier Aeroflot. After the crash, Aeroflot said it would cooperate fully with investigators and review safety procedures.

### High-profile victims

Among those killed was **Gen. Gennady Troshev**, a former Russian military commander known for his role in the Chechen wars, according to Russian officials and state media.

The crash was one of the deadliest in Russia in recent years and drew renewed attention to the country’s aviation safety record, particularly among smaller regional carriers and subsidiaries operating aging fleets or aircraft acquired secondhand from foreign airlines.

Aeroflot, once synonymous in the West with Soviet-era service and poor safety standards, has spent much of the past two decades trying to modernize its image. The airline has purchased Western aircraft, joined international alliances and sought to bring its operations closer to European standards. Its mainline safety record has improved markedly since the chaotic years following the collapse of the Soviet Union, when underfunded carriers, weak regulation and obsolete aircraft contributed to a series of deadly crashes across Russia and other former Soviet republics.

But the broader Russian aviation sector has remained uneven. Regional airlines have often faced financial pressure, pilot-training concerns and maintenance challenges, particularly when operating mixed fleets of Russian and Western aircraft. Safety experts have said that while aircraft age alone is not a determining factor in crashes, maintenance quality, crew training and regulatory oversight are critical.

Aeroflot-Nord, based in Arkhangelsk in northern Russia, had operated flights under a code-sharing and branding arrangement with Aeroflot. After the Perm crash, Russian media and aviation analysts questioned whether passengers understood the distinction between Aeroflot’s mainline service and flights operated by regional affiliates using the Aeroflot name.

“This is not simply a question of one aircraft,” said a Moscow-based aviation analyst. “It raises questions about supervision, training standards and how major carriers control the quality of partner airlines operating under their brand.”

Officials did not immediately report adverse weather as the primary cause. Perm airport authorities said the aircraft had been cleared for landing before contact was lost. Russian news agencies quoted air-traffic-control sources as saying the crew had acknowledged landing instructions, then disappeared from radar.

Investigators were expected to focus on the crew’s final communications, the aircraft’s altitude and speed, and whether the pilots may have become disoriented during the approach. They also were expected to examine maintenance records, fuel quality, crew schedules and the airline’s training procedures for Boeing aircraft.

The Boeing 737 is one of the world’s most widely used commercial aircraft families, with thousands in service globally. The 737-500, part of the “Classic” generation, has been operated extensively by airlines around the world since the late 1980s. Aviation specialists said the model has a long service history and that a crash investigation would likely center on the specific aircraft, operator and circumstances rather than the type itself.

Relatives of passengers gathered at Moscow’s Sheremetyevo airport and at Perm’s airport seeking information. Emergency officials said crisis counselors and medical staff were sent to assist families. A hotline was established, and authorities said identification of victims could take time because of the force of the impact and subsequent fire.

“At this moment, our main task is to help the families and recover the remains with dignity,” a Perm regional official said. “The investigation is under way, and every version will be examined.”

The crash occurred during a period of rapid growth in Russian air travel, fueled by rising incomes and expanding domestic routes linking Moscow with regional centers. But infrastructure, regulatory oversight and airline consolidation have struggled to keep pace.

Russia has suffered several major air disasters since the early 2000s, including crashes involving Tupolev and Airbus aircraft operated by domestic carriers. Each accident has prompted calls for tougher oversight, better pilot training and the retirement of outdated aircraft, though implementation has been inconsistent.

For Aeroflot, the Perm disaster posed a reputational challenge even though the flight was operated by its regional affiliate. The main carrier has worked aggressively to distance itself from the Soviet-era perception of Aeroflot as a sprawling state monopoly with a troubled safety record. It has introduced Western-built aircraft, adopted modern reservation systems and marketed itself as a global airline.

Still, in Russia’s complex aviation market, brand-sharing arrangements can blur responsibility in the eyes of passengers.

“If the ticket says Aeroflot, the public will see it as Aeroflot,” the aviation analyst said. “That is why the response from the parent company and regulators will be closely watched.”

Russian authorities said a preliminary report would be issued after analysis of the flight recorders and examination of evidence from the crash site. Full accident investigations can take months or longer, especially when they involve technical assistance from foreign manufacturers and investigators.

For now, officials said, there was no indication of terrorism.

“Initial evidence does not suggest an act of terror,” an investigative official said. “The main lines of inquiry concern the technical condition of the aircraft and the actions of the crew.”

As night fell in Perm, recovery workers continued searching the burned crash site under floodlights. Flowers and candles appeared near the airport and at public buildings in the city.

“All of Perm is grieving,” a local resident said. “People here were waiting for relatives, for friends, for colleagues. No one came home.”
